(i) No change in pressure: both gases are at the same temperature and pressure, so mixing just spreads the same total amount over the total volume.

(ii) The pressure decreases: 3 mol of gas (CO + 2H2) become 1 mol of CH3OH, so fewer gas molecules.

Measure the pressure, volume and temperature of the gas (as well as its mass).

Use pV = nRT to find n = pV/RT (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, with p in Pa, V in m³, T in K).

Then M = m/n, i.e. M = mRT/(pV).

At constant pressure, V/T is constant (Charles' law); temperatures must be in kelvin: 5 °C = 278 K, 25 °C = 298 K.

V2 = 955 × 298/278 = 1024 cm³ (≈1020 cm³)

1024 < 1100 cm³, so the balloon will not burst.

Any two: the particles gain kinetic energy (move faster); they collide with the balloon walls more frequently and more forcefully; so the balloon expands (particles spread out) to keep the pressure constant.
The pressure is unchanged. From pV = nRT with n and R constant, p ∝ T/V. Doubling T alone would double p, and doubling V alone would halve p. Together: p × 2 × ½ = p.

The pressure of methane is greater. Equal masses means methane contains twice as many moles (molecules), and its molecules also move faster, so there are more frequent collisions with the walls. From pV = nRT, p ∝ n at the same V and T.

n(O2) = 2.00 / 32.00 = 0.0625 mol; T = 298 K; V = 1.00 × 10−3 m3

p = nRT/V = 0.0625 × 8.31 × 298 / 1.00 × 10−3 = 1.55 × 105 Pa = 155 kPa (1.53 atm).

Watch the units: use dm3 with kPa, or m3 with Pa.

• The pressure in A is higher.
  • H2 has a much lower Mr, so 2.00 g contains more moles (1.00 mol vs 0.0625 mol) and more molecules. This gives more frequent collisions with the container walls at the same V and T.

2 mol Ba(NO3)2 give 5 mol gas (4NO2 + O2), so n(gas) = 0.010 × 5/2 = 0.025 mol.

V = nRT/p = 0.025 × 8.31 × 387 / 1.12 × 105 = 7.2 × 10−4 m3 = 720 cm3

Remember: Pa with m3, and 1 m3 = 106 cm3.

M = mass × Vm ÷ V = 1.00 g × 22 400 cm3 mol−1 ÷ 385 cm3 = 58.2 g mol−1 (or use pV = nRT).

The empirical formula mass of C2H5 is 29.1, and 58.2 ÷ 29.1 = 2, so the molecular formula is C4H10.

Note: the current data booklet uses 22.7 dm3 at STP, which gives M ≈ 59 and the same answer.

(iii) n(N2) = 1.00 × 3/2 = 1.50 mol
T = 25.00 + 273.15 = 298.15 K
p = 1.08 × 1.01 × 105 Pa = 1.09 × 105 Pa

Any one: at high pressure the particles are close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the container volume; at low temperature particles move slowly, so intermolecular attractive forces become significant.
Pressure is proportional to the number of gas moles (constant T and V). 2 mol of gas (2N2O) produce 3 mol (2N2 + O2), so the pressure increases by 50 % (from 2 to 3 – e.g. 200 → 300 units).

(i) C(NH2)3NO3(s) → 2N2(g) + 3H2O(g) + C(s).

(iv) Water is polar and forms hydrogen bonds — much stronger intermolecular forces than the London forces between non-polar N2. On cooling, water molecules attract/condense and occupy a smaller volume, so they deviate from ideal behaviour.
